name: Indexing a string
desc: A string is a sequence of characters. Counting starts at 0, and -1 is the last one.
code:
name = "Analytics"

print(name[0])
print(name[4])
print(name[-1])
print(len(name))

name: Slicing  [start:stop]
desc: Take a piece. The stop is NOT included, so [0:4] gives characters 0, 1, 2 and 3.
code:
name = "Analytics"

print(name[0:4])
print(name[:4])
print(name[4:])
print(name[-3:])

name: The third number  —  step
desc: How big a jump to take. A negative step walks backwards, which is how you reverse a string.
code:
name = "Analytics"

print(name[::2])
print(name[1::2])
print(name[::-1])        # reversed

name: A string cannot be changed
desc: Unlike a list, you cannot assign to one character. Build a new string instead.
code:
name = "Analytics"
name[0] = "X"
out: TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment

name: Joining and repeating
desc: + joins two strings, * repeats one. Both make a NEW string.
code:
a, b = "Data", "Analytics"
print(a + " " + b)
print("-" * 20)
print(a * 3)

name: in  —  is it there?
desc: Checks whether one string appears inside another. Hands back True or False.
code:
s = "Data Analytics"
print("Data" in s)
print("Python" in s)
print("data" in s)      # case matters

name: Changing case
desc: Four of them, and none of them change the original — they all hand back a new string.
code:
s = "data analytics"
print(s.upper())
print(s.title())
print(s.capitalize())
print("HELLO".lower())
print(s)        # untouched
out:
DATA ANALYTICS
Data Analytics
Data analytics
hello
data analytics

name: strip()  —  removing stray spaces
desc: The one you will use most on real data. Takes whitespace off both ends.
code:
s = "   Rahul Sharma   "
print("[" + s + "]")
print("[" + s.strip() + "]")
print("[" + s.lstrip() + "]")
print("[" + s.rstrip() + "]")
out:
[   Rahul Sharma   ]
[Rahul Sharma]
[Rahul Sharma   ]
[   Rahul Sharma]

name: replace()
desc: Swaps every occurrence of one piece of text for another.
code:
s = "Data Analytics"
print(s.replace("Data", "Business"))
print("a-b-c".replace("-", " "))
print(s.replace("a", "*"))
out:
Business Analytics
a b c
D*t* An*lytics

name: split()  and  join()
desc: split cuts a string into a list; join glues a list back into a string. Opposites.
code:
s = "HR,Tech,Sales"
parts = s.split(",")
print(parts)

print(" | ".join(parts))
print("Rahul Kumar Sharma".split())     # no argument = split on spaces

name: find()  and  count()
desc: find gives the POSITION of the first match, or -1 if it is not there. count gives how many.
code:
s = "statistics"
print(s.find("t"))
print(s.find("z"))        # -1, not an error
print(s.count("t"))
print(s.count("s"))

name: startswith / endswith
desc: Checks the beginning or the end. Handy for filenames and codes.
code:
f = "employees.csv"
print(f.endswith(".csv"))
print(f.startswith("emp"))
print("EMP1001".startswith("EMP"))

name: The is... checks
desc: Each one asks a yes/no question about what the string contains.
code:
print("12345".isdigit())
print("Rahul".isalpha())
print("Rahul123".isalnum())
print("   ".isspace())
print("HELLO".isupper())

name: f-strings
desc: Put an f before the quote and anything in curly brackets is worked out and dropped in.
code:
name, dept, salary = "Rahul", "HR", 47764

print(f"{name} works in {dept} and earns {salary}")
print(f"next year: {salary * 1.1}")
out:
Rahul works in HR and earns 47764
next year: 52540.4

name: Rounding inside an f-string
desc: :.2f means two decimal places. This is how you stop a salary printing as 52540.400000000001.
code:
salary = 47764
hiked = salary * 1.1

print(f"raw     {hiked}")
print(f"rounded {hiked:.2f}")
print(f"no dp   {hiked:.0f}")

name: Lining things up
desc: A number after < > or ^ sets the width, which is how you get columns that line up.

name: format()  —  the older way
desc: You will still meet this in older code. The curly brackets are filled in order.
code:
print("{} works in {}".format("Rahul", "HR"))
print("{1} then {0}".format("second", "first"))
print("{:.2f}".format(3.14159))
out:
Rahul works in HR
first then second
3.14

name: What a meta character is
desc: A character that means something other than itself. These are the ones that matter.
code:
print(r"\d   any digit 0-9")
print(r"\w   any letter, digit or underscore")
print(r"\s   any space, tab or newline")
print(r".    any character at all")
print(r"^    start of the string")
print(r"$    end of the string")
print(r"+    one or more")
print(r"*    zero or more")
print(r"?    zero or one")
print(r"{n}  exactly n of them")
out:
\d   any digit 0-9
\w   any letter, digit or underscore
\s   any space, tab or newline
.    any character at all
^    start of the string
$    end of the string
+    one or more
*    zero or more
?    zero or one
{n}  exactly n of them

name: re.findall()
desc: Finds EVERY match and hands them back as a list. The one you will use most.
code:
import re

s = "Rahul 1001, Priya 1002, Amit 1003"
print(re.findall(r"\d+", s))
print(re.findall(r"[A-Z][a-z]+", s))

name: re.search()
desc: Finds the FIRST match anywhere and hands back a match object, or None.
code:
import re

s = "Employee ID is EMP1001"
m = re.search(r"EMP\d+", s)
print(m)
print(m.group())
print(re.search(r"XYZ", s))      # None

name: re.match()  —  only at the start
desc: Same as search, but it only looks at the beginning of the string.
code:
import re

print(re.match(r"EMP", "EMP1001"))
print(re.match(r"1001", "EMP1001"))     # None - not at the start

name: re.sub()  —  find and replace
desc: Replaces every match with something else. A find-and-replace that understands patterns.
code:
import re

s = "Call 9876543210 or 9123456789"
print(re.sub(r"\d", "X", s))
print(re.sub(r"\d{10}", "[hidden]", s))
out:
Call XXXXXXXXXX or XXXXXXXXXX
Call [hidden] or [hidden]

name: re.split()
desc: Splits on a pattern rather than on one fixed character.
code:
import re

print(re.split(r"[,;]", "HR,Tech;Sales,Marketing"))
print(re.split(r"\s+", "too    many     spaces"))

name: A real check  —  is this an email?
desc: Putting the pieces together. ^ and $ mean the WHOLE string has to match, not just part of it.
code:
import re

pattern = r"^[\w.]+@[\w]+\.[a-z]{2,}$"

for e in ["rahul@tap.com", "priya.s@tap.co.in", "not-an-email", "a@b"]:
    print(e.ljust(20), bool(re.match(pattern, e)))
out:
rahul@tap.com        True
priya.s@tap.co.in    False
not-an-email         False
a@b                  False
